docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Cross-cutting ideas, trends, and frameworks in market research:

Page First Observed Last Updated Description ai-democratization 2026-06-24 2026-06-27 AI democratization refers to the process where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans. ai-professionalization 2026-06-24 2026-06-28 AI professionalization refers to the process where AI automates less expert tasks, leaving more expert tasks for humans. superstar-effect 2026-06-24 2026-06-27 The top 20% of most AI-exposed companies, referred to as 'superstars', achieve a significantly higher productivity growth rate. seniorised-roles 2026-06-25 2026-06-27 The phenomenon where entry-level roles increasingly demand skills traditionally required in senior positions due to AI adoption. ai-job-future-framework 2026-06-26 2026-06-27 A framework of four questions to analyze how AI is reshaping specific occupations, developed by PwC in their 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer. value-chain-shift 2026-06-28 2026-07-03 The value chain shift refers to the fundamental repositioning of where value is created within market research and insights organizations as AI capabilities advance. human-operating-model-gap 2026-06-28 2026-07-03 The human operating model gap refers to the growing disparity between the rapid advancement of AI capabilities and the slower adaptation of human systems, processes, and skills required to leverage AI effectively within organizations. entry-level-squeeze 2026-06-28 2026-07-03 The entry-level squeeze describes the growing pressure on traditional entry-level positions in knowledge work as AI capabilities automate foundational tasks that historically served as training grounds for developing professional expertise. capacity-hostile-environments 2026-07-03 2026-08-26 Environments that restrict, limit, or create a narrow field of affordances for the development and exercise of core human capacities, as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. These environments afford opportunities for shallow skilling while restricting fuller development of capacities, with significant implications for AI's impact on human flourishing. Expanded with detailed analysis of mechanisms, examples, and mitigation strategies from Ferdman's research, including specific market research applications and AI tool evaluation criteria. capacity-conducive-environments 2026-07-03 2026-08-26 Environments that actively encourage the development and exercise of human capacities through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing, providing alternatives to capacity-hostile conditions. These environments afford structured and unstructured embodied interactions necessary for intersubjective habituation of capacities. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, examples, and implementation strategies from Ferdman's research, including specific market research applications and organizational design principles. agential-control 2026-07-03 2026-08-26 The ability to adjust the execution of an action as the performance unfolds, a key component of being skilled that distinguishes skills from habits, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Skills require control over initiating the task, whereas habits are merely triggered by environmental cues. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, contrast with habitual action, market research implications, and AI tool design considerations from Ferdman's research. habituation-process 2026-07-03 2026-08-26 The gradual process of becoming skilled through practice, involving inculcation through continued attunement to demands of individual cases, with critical implications for AI's impact on skill development. Skill development cannot be learned through testimony alone but requires practice, encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, components, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. intersubjectivity-in-skilling 2026-07-03 2026-08-26 The shared understanding dimension of skill development, where learning occurs through relationships with others who guide and share the value of the skill. Becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to instill not only mechanical aspects but also the value of the skill. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, societal dimension, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. embodiment-in-skilling 2026-07-03 2026-08-26 The essential role of physical presence and sensory experience in the development of human capacities, particularly social and moral skills. Embodied interaction is critical for recognizing others as moral agents and forming meaningful relationships. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, contrast with disembodied interaction, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. ai-deskilling-structural-problem 2026-07-03 2026-08-26 The phenomenon where AI systems undermine human capacities through systemic conditions that create environments hostile to capacity cultivation, as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. This should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions, not merely an individual responsibility issue. Expanded with detailed analysis of mechanisms, examples, implications, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. ai-adoption-selection-bias 2026-07-03 2026-07-10 The substantial pre-existing differences between AI adopters and non-adopters that complicate causal inference in AI impact studies. ai-adoption-methodological-innovation 2026-07-03 2026-07-10 Methodological advances in measuring AI adoption, particularly the shift from occupational exposure scores to direct firm-level spending data. methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies 2026-07-03 2026-07-10 The challenge that different AI adoption measurement approaches yield dramatically different findings about AI's economic impact. pepm-metric 2026-07-15 2026-07-15 PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) metric measures the intensity of AI adoption at the firm level by calculating monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after sustained adoption begins. ai-adoption-intensity-terciles 2026-07-15 2026-07-15 Methodology categorizing firms based on AI adoption intensity, dividing them into high (top tercile) and low (bottom two terciles) intensity groups based on PEPM metric. developmental-perfectionism 2026-07-15 2026-08-26 Neo-Aristotelian approach to human flourishing where flourishing is understood as a complex, unified, and well-rounded life, providing the philosophical foundation for understanding why capacity-deskilling is harmful. Expanded with detailed analysis of principles, capacity connections, market research implications, and AI evaluation criteria from Ferdman's research. human-capacities 2026-07-15 2026-08-26 Core abilities that constitute human flourishing, including epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities, which are fundamental to being human and can be undermined by AI systems. Expanded with detailed analysis of core capacities, importance, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. plan-forming-vs-plan-following 2026-07-17 2026-08-26 The distinction between actively creating plans through self-deliberation (requiring agential control) versus executing pre-determined plans (more habitual), with critical implications for AI's impact on capacity development as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, AI's impact, market research implications, and mitigation strategies from Ferdman's research. narrow-field-of-affordances 2026-07-17 2026-08-26 An environment that provides limited action possibilities, restricting opportunities for the development and exercise of human capacities, a key mechanism through which AI systems can create capacity-hostile environments as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, mechanisms, examples, mitigation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. epistemic-capacities 2026-07-18 2026-08-26 The human capacities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding, including theoretical rationality and practical rationality (phronesis), which are essential for navigating truth and making informed decisions. Expanded with detailed analysis of components, importance, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. social-capacities 2026-07-18 2026-08-26 The human capacities related to forming meaningful relationships, understanding others' perspectives, and participating in communal life, including moral capacity and relational capacity. Expanded with detailed analysis of components, embodiment requirement, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. creative-capacities 2026-07-18 2026-08-26 The human capacities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces, which enable innovation and adaptation. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, connection to planning, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. volitional-capacity 2026-07-18 2026-08-26 The human capacity to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow in order to achieve intrinsically valuable goals, treated as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, connection to capacity development, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. plan-following 2026-07-25 2026-08-26 Plan-following refers to the execution of pre-determined plans without exercising agential control over the planning process itself. As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this represents a habitual mode of action where individuals respond to environmental triggers rather than initiating and adjusting plans through self-deliberation. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, contrast with plan-forming, AI's role, market research implications, and mitigation strategies from Ferdman's research.

Shows high-intensity adopters grow headcount by 10.2% and entry-level roles by 12.0%. ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem 2026-07-10 2026-08-26 Avigail Ferdman's 2026 paper in AI & Society presenting a structural analysis of how AI systems can undermine human capacities through systemic environmental conditions rather than individual failings. Introduces the critical distinction between capacity-hostile and capacity-conducive environments, analyzes the role of agential control and habituation in capacity development, and examines how Artificial Personal Assistants may create capacity-hostile environments by encouraging plan-following rather than plan-forming. The paper argues that deskilling should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions rather than merely an individual responsibility issue. Expanded with detailed analysis of methodology, key findings, market research implications, specific examples, and evaluation frameworks for AI tools.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Initiation Control: Skilled agents have full control over initiating activities, while habitual activities respond to environmental triggers
  • Adjustment Capability: Ability to modify performance in response to unfolding circumstances
  • Self-Deliberation: Involves active consideration of options rather than automatic response
  • Responsibility Taking: When plans fail, skilled agents take responsibility and learn, rather than shifting blame
  • Future Orientation: Connects present actions to future goals through intentional planning

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text:
1. Research Design: AI tools that preserve researchers' ability to initiate and adjust research approaches support agential control, while those that generate complete research plans encourage plan-following

  2. Client Relationships: Researchers maintaining agential control can better adapt to client needs in real-time, creating more valuable insights than those following rigid AI-generated protocols

  3. Team Development: Junior researchers develop faster in environments where they exercise agential control over research decisions rather than following AI recommendations

  4. Innovation Capacity: Market research organizations preserving agential control among staff are better positioned to develop novel methodologies in response to changing market conditions

docs.title: AI Tool Evaluation Criteria
docs.text:
When assessing research technology, organizations should consider:

  • Does the tool require researchers to initiate the research process, or does it present pre-formed recommendations?
  • Can researchers adjust the AI's suggestions based on unfolding research findings?
  • When research approaches fail, does the tool support learning or encourage blame-shifting?
  • Does the tool preserve opportunities for researchers to develop practical wisdom through experience?

As Ferdman argues, AI systems that encourage plan-following rather than plan-forming create capacity-hostile environments that undermine researchers' ability to exercise agential control—the very foundation of skilled research practice.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: AI Adoption Intensity Terciles is a methodology developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to categorize firms based on the intensity of their AI adoption, measured by the PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) metric.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. Firms are classified as AI adopters when they have three consecutive months of at least $100 in AI vendor spending
  2. Adoption intensity is measured as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over the first three months after adoption
  3. Among treated firms, PEPM values are sorted and divided into three equal groups (terciles):
  4. High intensity: top tercile (most intensive AI adopters)
  5. Medium intensity: middle tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom tercile (least intensive AI adopters)
  7. For analysis, firms are often grouped as:
  8. High intensity: top tercile
  9. Low intensity: bottom two terciles combined

docs.title: Rationale for Tercile Approach
docs.text:
• Allows researchers to examine differential impacts of AI adoption based on intensity
  • Reveals that not all AI adopters experience the same employment effects
  • Helps address selection bias by comparing firms with similar eventual adoption intensity
  • Shows that substantial employment gains are concentrated among high-intensity adopters

docs.title: Key Findings Using Intensity Terciles
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters grew total employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • High-intensity gains emerged gradually over 18-24 months, suggesting a learning curve
  • Employment gains were broad across roles for high-intensity adopters (engineering, sales, administration, customer service)

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: This methodology revealed a critical insight often missed in prior research: AI's labor market effects differ substantially based on adoption intensity. Studies that treat all adopters the same may miss these nuanced patterns.

docs.text: Methodological advances in measuring AI adoption, particularly the shift from occupational exposure scores to direct firm-level spending data. The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study represents a breakthrough in this area by using observed AI vendor payments rather than theoretical exposure metrics.

docs.title: Ramp-Revelio Methodology
docs.text:
The study introduces the AI Spend Per Employee Methodology (PEPM):

  1. Adoption definition: Three consecutive months of ≥$100 AI vendor spend
  2. Intensity measure: PEPM = (sum of first 3 months' AI spend) / (3 × baseline headcount)
  3. Intensity stratification: Low (bottom two PEPM terciles), High (top PEPM tercile)
  4. Comparison design: Later adopters within same intensity group

This approach overcomes four critical limitations of prior methods:

  1. Direct observation: Measures actual adoption behavior rather than theoretical exposure
  2. Timing precision: Captures exact adoption month rather than imputed timing
  3. Intensity dimension: Reveals differential effects by adoption intensity
  4. Firm-level specificity: Avoids occupational aggregation that masks firm differences

docs.title: Observed Spending Threshold
docs.text: The $100/month threshold excludes one-off experiments while capturing sustained adoption, addressing the "Is this really AI adoption?" question that plagues survey-based approaches.

docs.title: PEPM Metric
docs.text: Using baseline headcount in the denominator makes intensity comparable across firm sizes and keeps employee scale predetermined relative to adoption timing.

docs.title: Staggered Treatment Design
docs.text: The Callaway-Sant'Anna framework accounts for heterogeneous treatment timing, avoiding biases in traditional event-study approaches.

docs.title: Evidence of Impact
docs.text: This methodological innovation revealed findings invisible to exposure-based studies: - Only high-intensity adopters (+10.2% headcount growth) showed significant employment effects - Entry-level roles grew 12.0% among high-intensity adopters, contradicting exposure-based predictions - Effects concentrated in Information sector (+13.4% growth), not uniformly distributed

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological shift has critical implications:

  • Vendor evaluation: Must measure actual usage intensity, not just adoption status
  • Impact assessment: Requires tracking spending patterns over time, not binary adoption
  • Benchmarking: Industry comparisons must account for intensity differences
  • ROI calculation: Benefits appear only above critical intensity thresholds

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This innovation directly addresses the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and explains the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies observed across research. It represents a critical advance over the pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index used in pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer.

docs.title: Practical Implementation
docs.text:
For market research organizations, adopting this methodological innovation means: - Tracking actual AI spending rather than adoption claims - Measuring intensity through normalized spending metrics - Comparing against firms with similar pre-adoption characteristics - Focusing on sustained usage patterns rather than initial adoption

Without these methodological improvements, organizations risk misattributing effects or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns—precisely what the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study demonstrates.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The substantial pre-existing differences between AI adopters and non-adopters that complicate causal inference in AI impact studies. As rigorously documented in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, these selection effects mean AI adopters were already distinct from non-adopters before AI adoption, creating significant methodological challenges.

docs.title: Key Evidence
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study demonstrates dramatic pre-adoption differences:

Characteristic AI Adopters Never Adopters Difference Headcount (mean) 144.2 103.9 +40.3* Engineering share 26.8% 18.6% +8.2* Entry-level share 42.1% 50.4% -8.3* YoY growth (median) 6.0% 1.6% +4.4* Mean salary $110,346 $93,847 +$16,499* Tech-adjacent sector 54.2% 25.9% +28.3* VC-backed 34.0% 9.5% +24.5*

*Statistically significant at p<0.01

docs.title: Methodological Implications
docs.text:
This selection bias creates three critical challenges for AI impact research:

  1. Confounded comparisons: Simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons conflate AI effects with pre-existing differences
  2. Pre-trend divergence: Adopters were already on different growth trajectories before adoption (see Figure 4 in Ramp-Revelio study)
  3. Sector concentration: AI adoption heavily concentrated in Information (53.7%), Finance (43.6%), and Professional Services (36.0%)

docs.title: Addressing the Bias
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study employs sophisticated methods to address selection bias:

  • Preferred comparison: Later adopters within the same eventual intensity group
  • Sector fixed effects: Controlling for industry composition differences
  • Event-time analysis: Tracking pre-treatment parallel trends
  • Intensity stratification: Separating low vs. high adoption intensity effects

This approach revealed that only high-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no significant change.

docs.title: Contrast with Exposure-Based Studies
docs.text: This selection bias explains why exposure-based studies (like pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer) often produce different findings than spending-based studies: - Exposure scores cannot distinguish firms that adopt AI from those that don't - They assume uniform adoption effects across firms with identical workforce composition - They miss the critical intensity dimension revealed by actual spending data

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This concept has profound implications for insights organizations:

  • Vendor selection: AI tools adopted by leading firms may reflect pre-existing advantages rather than causal benefits
  • Implementation strategy: Success depends on organizational readiness, not just tool adoption
  • Impact measurement: Must account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI initiatives
  • Benchmarking: Comparing against industry averages without controlling for selection effects is misleading

docs.text: This concept is central to understanding the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies problem and represents a key ai-adoption-methodological-innovation addressed by the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study. It explains why the employment gains documented in that study are concentrated among high-intensity adopters in specific sectors, rather than across all AI adopters.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, addressing selection bias requires: - Never comparing AI adopters to non-adopters without controlling for pre-existing differences - Measuring adoption intensity (PEPM) rather than binary adoption status - Using staggered adoption timing in evaluation designs - Focusing on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact

Without these precautions, organizations risk attributing pre-existing advantages to AI adoption or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns.

docs.title: Ai democratization
docs.text: AI democratization refers to the process where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI democratization describes how artificial intelligence makes advanced capabilities accessible by automating complex expert tasks, thereby reducing expertise requirements for certain occupations. As quantified in Figure 2 of the PwC 2026 report, this process affects 52% of global job postings. Concrete examples include [[recruiters]] (AI automates CV screening while humans handle contract negotiation) and [[inventory-clerks]] (AI manages stock optimization while humans perform physical movement). Figure 3 demonstrates democratization is particularly strong in high AI exposure jobs, where expertise requirements decrease significantly. Crucially, Figure 11 reveals that despite reduced expertise demands, democratized roles maintain high epoch-score (0.48), indicating continued reliance on human capabilities for remaining tasks—often involving physical dexterity, adaptability, or interpersonal skills. The report warns that while democratization expands job accessibility (e.g., enabling non-experts to perform data analysis), it may compress career ladders and reduce skill development opportunities without targeted interventions. This concept represents one of two primary pathways (alongside ai-professionalization) in AI's labor market restructuring. Organizations can leverage democratization through the ai-job-future-framework's 'Supply and Demand' dimension, redesigning roles to balance AI efficiency with human execution. The trend is accelerating post-2022, as shown in Figure 9's widening skill transformation gap, requiring proactive workforce planning to ensure equitable access to emerging opportunities in democratized roles.

docs.title: 2026-08-26 Update
docs.text: The phenomenon where AI systems undermine human capacities through systemic conditions that create environments hostile to capacity cultivation, as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. This should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions, not merely an individual responsibility issue.

docs.title: Core Argument
docs.text: Ferdman challenges the individual responsibility framing of AI-induced deskilling, arguing that: - Capacity cultivation depends on environmental conditions, not just individual will - AI systems create structural conditions that restrict opportunities for capacity development - Deskilling occurs through systemic environmental factors rather than individual failings - Solutions must address the structural conditions, not just individual adaptation

docs.title: Key Mechanisms
docs.text:
1. Narrow field of affordances: AI systems reduce action possibilities for capacity development
  2. Automation bias: Users attribute excessive trust to AI outputs over human judgment
  3. Plan-following encouragement: Systems convert plan-forming into plan-following behavior
  4. Disembodied interaction: Digital environments that replace embodied engagement
  5. Responsibility displacement: Users shift accountability for failures to AI systems

docs.title: Market Research Applications
docs.text: In market research, the structural deskilling problem manifests through: - AI tools that automate data interpretation, reducing opportunities to develop practical rationality - Remote research methods that eliminate embodied interaction essential for social capacity development - Automated reporting systems that create a narrow field of affordances for junior researchers - Algorithmic respondent matching that reduces opportunities to develop nuanced demographic understanding

docs.title: Evidence from Research
docs.text: Ferdman cites evidence that: - Heavy APA users show reduced development of practical rationality - Disembodied interaction requires more mental effort for moral attribution - Automation of routine tasks deprives users of "cognitive musculature" development - Plan-following behavior undermines the habituation process necessary for skill development

docs.title: Structural Solutions
docs.text: Rather than expecting individuals to be "virtuous superheroes," Ferdman proposes: - Designing AI systems that preserve opportunities for agential control - Creating hybrid workflows that maintain intersubjective mentorship - Developing organizational practices that encourage plan-forming - Implementing "capacity audits" for AI tools - Fostering environments that afford embodied interaction

docs.title: Connection to Market Research
docs.text:
The structural deskilling problem has profound implications for market research: - Threatens the industry's ability to produce genuinely human-centered insights - Undermines the development of junior researchers through reduced habituation opportunities - Creates capacity-hostile environments that devalue the "arts of personhood" - Requires industry-wide solutions rather than individual adaptation strategies

Ferdman's framework provides a critical lens for evaluating AI adoption in market research, emphasizing that efficiency gains must be balanced against potential capacity deskilling effects. Organizations must intentionally design AI systems that support rather than undermine the development of human capacities essential for quality research.

docs.title: Ai job future framework
docs.text: A framework of four questions to analyze how AI is reshaping specific occupations, developed by PwC in their 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The AI Job Future Framework, introduced in Figure 6 of PwC's 2026 report, provides a structured methodology to assess AI's occupational impact through four critical questions: (1) Expertise: How is AI changing required human expertise? (e.g., democratization reduces expertise needs while professionalization increases them); (2) Supply and Demand: How might job demand and worker supply shift as AI reshapes roles?; (3) AI's limitations: Where is human oversight needed for quality control or atypical cases?; and (4) Environmental forces: How do regulations, business bottlenecks, or ethics constrain AI adoption? The report demonstrates the framework's application across diverse occupations: For [[pharmacists]], AI handles prescription processing (Expertise shift) but humans manage patient counseling (AI's limitations); for [[software-developers]], AI generates code but humans focus on architecture (Environmental forces). Figure 9 validates the framework by showing how high AI exposure roles undergo 2.2x faster skill changes, directly addressing the Supply and Demand dimension. Organizations using this tool can anticipate skill shifts, redesign roles, and develop targeted training—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' (Figure 12). The framework also explains wage dynamics: roles requiring human oversight of AI (Question 3) command higher premiums, as seen in Figure 15's 62% average AI skill premium. By systematically addressing these questions, employers can transform AI disruption into opportunity, while workers identify future-proof career paths in the evolving labor market. This methodology has become essential for strategic workforce planning in the AI era.

AI professionalization refers to the process where AI automates less expert tasks, leaving more expert tasks for humans. This phenomenon represents one pathway through which AI reshapes occupations, increasing the premium on specialized human expertise.

docs.title: New Evidence and Refinement
docs.text:
The mrii-2026-market-research-study provides compelling evidence of AI professionalization in the insights industry: - As AI handles routine analytical tasks, value is shifting upstream toward strategic functions - Insights teams must evolve from delivering answers to shaping decisions, driving growth, and influencing strategy - Pam Forbus of [[mondelez]] states: "AI will increasingly answer questions, deliver insights, execute projects, and support stakeholders faster and at lower cost than ever before. That doesn't diminish the role of insights teams; it fundamentally changes it."

This represents a specific manifestation of professionalization where AI automation of basic tasks elevates the importance of strategic human capabilities.

The value-chain-shift concept further explains this dynamic - as AI makes answers faster and cheaper, the answers themselves become less differentiated, pushing value creation toward higher-order strategic functions.

docs.title: Relationship to Skills Development
docs.text:
A critical finding from the MRII study reveals a professionalization paradox: - Professionals prioritize learning technical AI skills - Leaders value business acumen, communication, and strategic influence more highly

This disconnect threatens to undermine the professionalization process, as organizations may automate tasks without adequately developing the human capabilities needed for the elevated roles.

docs.title: Connection to Entry-Level Dynamics
docs.text: The burning-glass-beyond-binary report shows that professionalization occurs alongside automation within the same occupations. This creates particular challenges for entry-level positions through the entry-level-squeeze, as foundational tasks that build expertise are automated before new developmental pathways are established.

docs.title: Organizational Implications
docs.text: Successful navigation of AI professionalization requires: - Redesigning roles to preserve meaningful human involvement in value-creating activities - Developing new apprenticeship models that build expertise despite automated foundational tasks - Aligning skill development priorities with the evolving value chain

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Rich Affordance Field: Provide diverse action possibilities that trigger multiple human capacities simultaneously
  • Embodied Interaction Support: Create opportunities for physical presence and sensory experience essential for social capacity development
  • Intersubjective Habituation: Facilitate mentorship relationships where both mechanical aspects and value of skills are transmitted
  • Agential Control Preservation: Maintain opportunities for initiating and adjusting activities rather than merely responding to environmental triggers
  • Gradual Skill Development: Support the habituation process through successive trials, mistakes, and refinement

docs.title: Implementation Strategies in Market Research
docs.text:
1. AI-Augmented Rather Than AI-Replaced Processes: Design research workflows where AI handles routine tasks but preserves opportunities for researchers to develop judgment in complex scenarios

  2. Embodied Research Methods: Maintain face-to-face qualitative research components even when supplemented with AI analysis tools

  3. Structured Mentorship Programs: Create formal opportunities for senior researchers to guide juniors through the habituation process, emphasizing not just "how" but "why" certain research approaches have value

  4. Deliberate Skill Development Frameworks: Implement research project structures that intentionally expose researchers to progressively more complex challenges

  5. Shared Valuing Mechanisms: Establish team practices that reinforce the intrinsic value of research capacities beyond mere task completion

docs.title: Market Research Applications
docs.text:
• Hybrid Research Design: Combine AI-powered data collection with human-led interpretation sessions where researchers practice theoretical and practical rationality

  • AI-Assisted Debriefing: Use AI to generate initial analysis but require researchers to refine and adjust interpretations, preserving agential control

  • Embodied Client Workshops: Design research engagements that include in-person co-creation sessions, using AI to prepare materials but not replace human interaction

  • Failure Analysis Rituals: Create team practices for examining research missteps, turning disappointments into habituation opportunities

  • Capacity-Conducive Tool Selection: Evaluate research technology through Ferdman's framework, prioritizing tools that encourage rather than merely afford capacity development

As Ferdman emphasizes, capacity-conducive environments will afford opportunities for cultivating the volitional-capacity, by encouraging agents to develop and exercise their other capacities without expecting them to be 'virtuous superheroes.' These environments recognize that developing capacities is difficult and requires supportive structures.

docs.title: Human operating model gap
docs.text: The human operating model gap refers to the growing disparity between the rapid advancement of AI capabilities and the slower adaptation of human systems, processes, and skills required to leverage AI effectively within organizations.

docs.title: Workforce Composition Changes with AI Adoption
docs.text: Recent evidence reveals how AI adoption is reshaping workforce composition across roles, highlighting the growing gap between rapidly advancing AI capabilities and slower human system adaptation.

docs.title: Role-Specific Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study provides detailed evidence of how AI adoption affects different job functions:

  • Broad-based growth: High-intensity adopters showed growth across multiple roles:
  • Sales headcount: +10.3%
  • Administrative headcount: +7.8%
  • Engineering headcount: +7.3%
  • Customer service headcount: +6.3%

  • Scientist headcount: +5.6%

  • Entry-level expansion: Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% among high-intensity adopters

  • Managerial shifts: Manager-plus share fell by 1.52 percentage points despite overall growth

docs.title: Structural Workforce Shifts
docs.text:
These findings reveal several important patterns:

  1. Non-binary impact: AI adoption doesn't simply eliminate jobs but reshapes workforce composition
  2. Intensity matters: Only high-intensity adopters (top tercile of AI spend) showed significant growth
  3. Gradual emergence: Gains followed a learning curve, emerging 6-12 months after adoption
  4. Sector concentration: Effects were strongest in the Information sector

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these workforce shifts suggest:

  • AI is currently augmenting rather than replacing human capabilities in information work
  • Strategic AI investment may support growth across multiple functions
  • Entry-level positions may expand as firms scale with AI assistance
  • Workforce planning must account for the gradual nature of AI integration

The study notes that "the earliest signs of growth emerge roughly 6-12 months after adoption, perhaps after firms establish best practices, integrate AI tools into workflows, and are subsequently able to make new investments and hire staff."

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The challenge that different AI adoption measurement approaches yield dramatically different findings about AI's economic impact. As demonstrated by the contrast between exposure-based studies and spending-based research like the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, methodological choices fundamentally shape conclusions about AI's labor market effects.

docs.title: Evidence of Heterogeneity
docs.text:
Study Type Primary Method Key Employment Finding Example Exposure-based Occupational AI exposure scores Negative impact on entry-level jobs Brynjolfsson et al. (2025) Spending-based Observed AI vendor payments Positive impact at high intensity Ramp-Revelio study Survey-based Executive adoption surveys Mixed or positive impacts Yotzov et al. (2026)

The Ramp-Revelio study documents this heterogeneity through direct comparison: - Exposure-based studies predict job losses in high-exposure occupations - Spending-based research shows job growth among high-intensity adopters - The discrepancy stems from methodological differences, not contradictory realities

docs.title: Root Causes
docs.text: Three fundamental methodological differences drive these divergent findings:

docs.title: 1. Adoption Measurement
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Measure theoretical task feasibility ("could AI do this?")
  • Spending data: Measure actual adoption behavior ("is the firm paying for AI?")
  • Surveys: Capture self-reported usage ("do executives say they use AI?")

As the Ramp-Revelio study notes: "These estimates are closer to the Ramp–Revelio paid-adoption series than the firm-weighted BTOS benchmark, but they still measure a different object."

docs.title: 2. Intensity Dimension
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Typically binary or quintile-based
  • Spending data: Reveals continuous intensity effects (PEPM metric)
  • Surveys: Often lack precise intensity measures

The Ramp-Revelio study found only high-intensity adopters showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no change.

docs.title: 3. Selection Bias Handling
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Cannot distinguish adopters from non-adopters with identical workforce
  • Spending data: Enables direct comparison of adopters vs. later adopters
  • Surveys: Often lack pre-adoption data for comparison

The Ramp-Revelio study documents substantial pre-adoption differences that confound simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological heterogeneity creates critical challenges:

  • Conflicting guidance: Different studies recommend opposite actions based on methodology
  • Implementation uncertainty: Hard to predict AI impact without knowing intensity threshold
  • Evaluation complexity: Must select appropriate methodology for specific context
  • Vendor claims: AI providers may cite favorable methodology while ignoring others

docs.title: Strategic Response Framework
docs.text:
Market research organizations should adopt a methodologically sophisticated approach:

  1. Triangulate findings: Consider evidence from multiple methodological approaches
  2. Assess intensity: Focus on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact
  3. Control for selection: Account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI
  4. Contextualize results: Recognize sector-specific effects (e.g., concentrated in Information)

docs.text: This concept explains the contradictory findings between the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study (showing 12.0% entry-level growth) and exposure-based studies predicting job losses. It represents the methodological foundation for understanding the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and the value of the ai-adoption-methodological-innovation in spending-based measurement.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, navigating methodological heterogeneity requires: - Never relying on a single study's methodology for decision-making - Understanding the measurement approach behind any AI impact claim - Recognizing that "AI adoption" has no single empirical rate (as shown in Ramp-Revelio Figure 1) - Focusing on high-intensity implementation thresholds rather than binary adoption

Without this methodological sophistication, organizations risk making decisions based on incomplete or misleading evidence about AI's true impact.

docs.text: Narrow fields of affordances develop through: 1. Initial automation of routine tasks 2. Gradual expansion to more complex activities 3. Systematic reduction of action possibilities across multiple spheres 4. Cumulative effect across multiple human activities 5. Discouragement of compensation strategies due to pervasive automation

Ferdman argues that addressing narrow fields of affordances requires structural solutions at the organizational level, not just individual adaptation. In market research specifically, organizations must intentionally design research workflows that maintain sufficient action possibilities for capacity development, recognizing that efficiency gains from AI must be balanced against potential capacity deskilling effects. Capacity-conducive research environments actively resist affordance shrinkage by preserving opportunities for researchers to engage fully with the research process, even when AI tools could automate certain aspects.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) is a metric developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to measure the intensity of AI adoption at the firm level. It calculates monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after sustained AI adoption begins.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
PEPM = (Σ²ₘ₌₀ AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ) / (3 × HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁)

Where: - AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ = AI vendor spend for firm i in month m after adoption - HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁ = baseline headcount in the month before adoption

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. AI adoption is defined as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  2. PEPM is calculated using AI spend over the first three months after adoption begins
  3. Baseline headcount is measured in the month before adoption
  4. Firms are sorted into intensity groups:
  5. High intensity: top PEPM tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom two PEPM terciles

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
• Provides a direct, observed measure of AI adoption intensity rather than relying on occupational exposure scores
  • Allows researchers to distinguish between firms that adopt AI lightly versus intensively
  • Correlates closely with adoption of more complex AI products and tools (coding agents, APIs) versus simpler chat subscriptions
  • Enables analysis of differential impacts based on adoption intensity

docs.title: Key Findings Using PEPM
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters (top tercile) grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • Gains emerged gradually, suggesting a "learning curve" as firms integrated AI tools

Capacity-conducive research environments maintain spaces where researchers must initiate and adjust their own research plans, even when AI tools provide valuable assistance with execution.

docs.title: Seniorised roles
docs.text: The phenomenon where entry-level roles increasingly demand skills traditionally required in senior positions due to AI adoption.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: Seniorised roles describe the accelerating trend where entry-level positions now require skills traditionally associated with senior roles, driven by AI automation of foundational tasks. Figure 8 in the PwC 2026 report provides compelling evidence: in the US top AI exposure quartile, seniorised entry-level job postings are projected to grow 35% between 2019-2025, while non-seniorised roles decline by 10%. This occurs because AI tools handle routine onboarding tasks (e.g., data entry for [[inventory-clerks]] or basic analysis for [[recruiters]]), compressing career ladders and elevating entry requirements. Common senior skills now appearing in entry-level descriptions include strategic decision-making frameworks, cross-departmental collaboration, client advisory capabilities, and complex problem-solving—particularly in high-growth professionalised-jobs. Figure 7 contextualizes this within broader market trends, showing high AI exposure quartile entry-level postings have flatlined since 2022, suggesting seniorisation may be a prerequisite for growth in AI-impacted roles. The report warns this trend could exacerbate early-career inequality if not balanced with structured mentorship, as new graduates face higher barriers without prior exposure to advanced skills. However, organizations using the ai-job-future-framework can mitigate risks by designing onboarding that combines AI tools with human skill development. The phenomenon represents a key manifestation of AI's impact on career progression, with implications for education systems needing to prepare students for accelerated responsibility in the AI era.

docs.title: Superstar effect
docs.text: The top 20% of most AI-exposed companies, referred to as 'superstars', achieve a significantly higher productivity growth rate.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The 'superstar effect' identifies a critical divergence among AI adopters: the top 20% of most AI-exposed firms achieve dramatically higher productivity gains than peers. This effect was documented by pwc using orbis company financial data. As revealed in Figure 12 of the PwC 2026 report, these 'superstar' companies attained 163% average productivity growth in 2025—5 times higher than the 33.5% growth rate of most AI-exposed companies as a whole. This advantage has widened steadily since 2022, with superstars accelerating their lead while other AI-exposed firms maintain moderate growth. Figure 13 shows this productivity advantage translates to headcount growth, with superstar firms expanding employment 52.2% by 2025 versus 35.7% for least exposed quartiles. Crucially, Figure 14 demonstrates these gains are shared with workers through higher wage growth (24.4% vs 16.6% in 2025). The report attributes superstar status to three factors: strategic AI integration beyond automation (leveraging the ai-job-future-framework), investment in complementary human skills, and organizational agility in addressing [[ai's limitations]]. This creates a 'winner-takes-most' dynamic where superstars capture disproportionate value—evident in Figure 16's AI specialist hiring surge within these firms. The effect has profound implications: companies failing to achieve superstar status risk falling behind in the AI transformation, while workers in superstar firms gain through both wages and career opportunities in high-growth professionalised-jobs. Policymakers must address resulting market concentration through targeted support for mid-tier AI adopters.

docs.title: Value chain shift
docs.text: The value chain shift refers to the fundamental repositioning of where value is created within market research and insights organizations as AI capabilities advance.

docs.title: Sectoral Variations in AI Impact
docs.text: Recent research reveals that AI's impact on the value chain is unevenly distributed across sectors, with significant implications for how value is created within market research organizations.

docs.title: Sectoral Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study found that employment gains from AI adoption are concentrated in the Information sector:

  • Information sector: 13.4% headcount growth among high-intensity AI adopters
  • Professional and technical services: Positive but non-significant growth
  • All other sectors: Near-zero or imprecise effects

This pattern reflects the current state of AI adoption, which is "uniquely concentrated in Information" where "the most commercially mature AI gains appear clearest in coding-agent and software-engineering workflows."

docs.title: Implications for Market Research Value Chain
docs.text:
For market research firms, this sectoral variation suggests:

  1. Front-end transformation: Research design and data collection may see earlier AI integration
  2. Back-end resilience: Interpretation and strategic recommendation may remain more human-intensive
  3. Specialization opportunities: Firms focusing on information-intensive research may adopt AI more rapidly
  4. Competitive differentiation: Early AI adopters in research may gain productivity advantages

The study notes that "it is still early in the AI adoption curve" and "AI use cases may diffuse more slowly outside software and media." This suggests market research firms should anticipate a gradual shift in where value is created, rather than an immediate transformation.

docs.title: Strategic Considerations
docs.text:
Market research organizations should consider:

  • Where their work aligns with sectors experiencing the strongest AI impacts
  • How to position themselves to benefit from productivity gains in information processing
  • When to invest in high-intensity AI adoption versus more limited applications
  • How to develop workforce strategies that align with sector-specific AI adoption patterns

  2. Agential Control Preservation: Design workflows where researchers must initiate and adjust AI recommendations

  3. Embodied Counterbalance: Ensure AI-assisted planning is followed by face-to-face team discussions

  4. Failure Integration: Create opportunities to examine where AI recommendations proved inadequate

  5. Mentorship Enhancement: Use AI assistants to support rather than replace human mentorship relationships

As Ferdman warns, 'the more the APA does things for the user, the more it could constitute a capacity-hostile environment.' Market research organizations must carefully evaluate how AI personal assistants affect researchers' capacity development rather than focusing solely on short-term productivity gains.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Callaway-Sant'Anna framework is an econometric approach for analyzing treatment effects when units receive treatment at different times, as implemented in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to analyze the impact of AI adoption on employment.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• Developed by Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) to address limitations of conventional two-way fixed effects event studies
  • Designed for staggered adoption designs where firms begin treatment (AI adoption) at different points in time
  • Estimates group-time average treatment effects separately for different adoption cohorts
  • Compares earlier adopters to later adopters in the same intensity group while the later adopters have not yet adopted

docs.title: Implementation in Ramp-Revelio Study
docs.text:
• Used to estimate the relationship between firm-level AI adoption and employment
  • Applied separately to low and high AI intensity adoption groups
  • For high-intensity adopters, compared firms that adopted early to firms that would eventually be high-intensity adopters but hadn't yet adopted
  • Included NAICS sector fixed effects to address selection into early AI adoption

docs.title: Advantages Over Traditional Methods
docs.text:
• Better suited to heterogeneous treatment timing than single two-way fixed effects event studies
  • Reduces bias that can occur when treatment effects are heterogeneous across adoption cohorts
  • Allows for more precise estimation of dynamic treatment effects
  • Provides cleaner pre-treatment diagnostics for parallel trends assumption

docs.title: Key Findings Enabled by This Framework
docs.text:
• Revealed that high-intensity AI adopters grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Showed that these gains emerged gradually over 18-24 months
  • Demonstrated that low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • Provided evidence against predictions that AI adoption would lead to broad job losses

docs.title: Lightcast
docs.text: Lightcast (formerly Emsi Burning Glass) is a labor market analytics company that provides detailed data on job postings, skills demand, and workforce trends. The company aggregates and analyzes millions of job postings from across the internet to create comprehensive labor market intelligence.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: Lightcast data serves as a primary source for PwC's Global AI Jobs Barometer analysis. According to the 2026 report, the analysis examined over one billion online job advertisements across six continents, with Lightcast providing the underlying job posting data.

docs.title: Data Collection Methodology
docs.text:
Lightcast gathers job posting data through:

  • Web scraping of major job boards and company career sites
  • Partnerships with job posting aggregators
  • Direct feeds from some large employers
  • Historical archives dating back to 2012 for certain markets

The company processes this raw data to extract structured information about required skills, qualifications, compensation, and other job characteristics.

docs.title: Application in PwC's Research
docs.text:
In the PwC 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, Lightcast data was used to:

  • Track changes in job posting volumes across different AI exposure levels
  • Analyze skill requirements and how they evolve over time
  • Calculate wage premiums for AI-related skills
  • Identify trends in entry-level hiring patterns
  • Measure growth in AI specialist positions

docs.title: Key Insights Enabled by Lightcast Data
docs.text:
Analysis of Lightcast data revealed several critical patterns:

  • AI specialist job postings grew eight times faster than total job postings from 2012-2025
  • Entry-level job postings in the highest AI exposure quartile flatlined after 2022
  • Skills needed for the most AI-exposed jobs are changing 2.2x faster than for the least exposed jobs
  • Wage premiums for AI skills reached 62% across all sectors in 2025

docs.title: Limitations and Considerations
docs.text:
While valuable, Lightcast data has certain limitations:

  • Primarily captures formal, online job postings (may miss informal hiring)
  • Coverage varies by country and time period
  • Skill extraction relies on natural language processing of job descriptions
  • May not fully capture internal mobility or promotions

Researchers using Lightcast data, like PwC, typically note these limitations and adjust their methodologies accordingly.

See also: pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer, pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index

docs.title: ORBIS
docs.text: ORBIS is a comprehensive global business information database maintained by Bureau van Dijk (a Moody's Analytics company). It provides detailed financial, ownership, and operational data on millions of companies worldwide, serving as a critical resource for business intelligence and economic research.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: In PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, ORBIS data served as the primary source for company-level analysis, particularly regarding productivity, headcount, and wage growth metrics across different levels of AI exposure.

docs.title: Data Coverage
docs.text:
ORBIS includes information on:

  • Over 400 million companies globally
  • Financial statements and performance metrics
  • Ownership structures and corporate hierarchies
  • Industry classifications using standard systems like NAICS
  • Employment data and executive information

For the PwC analysis, the database provided longitudinal data from 2018-2025 for companies with consistent reporting.

docs.title: Application in PwC's Research
docs.text:
PwC used ORBIS data to:

  • Measure productivity growth (revenue per employee) across AI exposure levels
  • Track headcount changes at companies in different AI exposure quartiles
  • Analyze wage growth patterns relative to AI adoption
  • Identify the "superstar effect" among highly AI-exposed companies

docs.title: Key Insights Enabled by ORBIS Data
docs.text:
Analysis of ORBIS data revealed several critical patterns:

  • The most AI-exposed companies showed 33.5% productivity growth (2018-2025) compared to 18.7% for least exposed
  • Headcount growth at most AI-exposed companies reached 52.2% versus 23.3% for least exposed
  • Wage growth at most AI-exposed companies reached 24.4% versus 5.6% for least exposed
  • The top 20% of most AI-exposed companies ("superstars") achieved 163% productivity growth

docs.title: Methodological Considerations
docs.text:
PwC's analysis using ORBIS data included several important methodological notes:

  • Focus on larger formal firms with annual turnover of at least $50m USD
  • Exclusion of companies that exited the market during the period (creating survivorship bias)
  • Potential bias toward larger, more formalized companies in some countries
  • Company AI exposure determined by NAICS sector classification

These considerations mean the analysis reflects patterns among established businesses rather than the entire economy, but still provides valuable insights into how AI adoption correlates with business performance.

See also: pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer, superstar-effect

docs.title: PwC
docs.text: PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) is a multinational professional services network and one of the Big Four accounting firms. It provides audit and assurance, tax, and advisory services to corporations, governments, and non-profit organizations globally. With operations in 157 countries and over 360,000 employees, PwC serves as a leading authority on economic and labor market trends.

docs.title: Relevance to AI and Market Research
docs.text: PwC has emerged as a pivotal publisher of research on artificial intelligence's impact on the global labor market. Its annual Global AI Jobs Barometer report analyzes trends using data from over one billion job advertisements, providing critical insights for the market research industry. The firm's proprietary pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index methodology has become a standard for measuring AI's workforce impact.

docs.title: Key Contributions
docs.text:
• Developed the epoch-score framework for measuring human capability reliance in occupations
  • Identified the dual trends of ai-democratization (52% of jobs) and ai-professionalization (22% of jobs)
  • Documented the superstar-effect where top AI-adopting companies achieve disproportionate productivity gains
  • Quantified wage premiums for ai-skills across economic sectors

PwC's research directly informs talent strategy for market research firms navigating AI adoption. Their data provides empirical validation for skills gap analyses and workforce planning.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Ramp is a financial operations platform that processes corporate card and bill pay transactions. It provides the AI Index for measuring AI adoption intensity through corporate spending data.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: Ramp's data was central to the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, which linked Ramp's line-item spending data with Revelio Labs' workforce records to study AI's impact on employment.

docs.title: AI Index Methodology
docs.text:
• Identifies AI spend from line items using vendor and line-item classification
  • Captures spending on foundational large language models, GPU cloud, model serving and inference, coding agents, API tokens, AI image and video generators, and AI search and research software
  • Defines AI adoption as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  • Measures adoption intensity as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over first three months after adoption

docs.title: Data Collection
docs.text:
• Observes cleared spend at the line-item level, including date, amount, merchant, firm identifiers, and line-item detail
  • Aggregates records to the firm-month level
  • Requires firms to have at least six consecutive months of total Ramp spend of $5,000+ to qualify for analysis

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: Ramp's data provides a direct measure of AI adoption through actual spending, overcoming limitations of occupational exposure scores and surveys. This revealed-adoption measure captures firms making sustained, organization-level AI purchases rather than one-off employee experiments.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Revelio Labs is a workforce intelligence platform that aggregates data from online professional profiles to construct longitudinal employment histories. It provides seniority classification and workforce composition data.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: Revelio Labs' workforce data was central to the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, which linked Revelio's employment records with Ramp's AI spending data to study AI's impact on employment.

docs.title: Data Collection Methodology
docs.text:
• Aggregates information from millions of publicly available online professional profiles
  • Constructs longitudinal employment histories for individual workers
  • Each profile contains information on employers, job titles, employment dates, locations, and other career characteristics
  • Uses a seven-point seniority field to define:
  • Entry-level headcount: seniority 1-2
  • Non-entry headcount: seniority 3-7
  • Manager-plus headcount: seniority 4-7
  • Applies weighting methodology to adjust for differential platform usage and improve representativeness

docs.title: Data Validation
docs.text:
• Prior validation exercises show weighted Revelio measures closely track benchmark labor market statistics
  • Similar worker-level employment histories have been used extensively in academic research

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: Revelio Labs provides granular workforce data that enables analysis of not just total firm employment but also hiring, attrition, occupational composition, worker seniority, and other workforce characteristics difficult to observe in traditional data sources.

docs.title: AI Spend Per Employee Methodology
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-03

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A direct measurement approach for quantifying firm-level AI adoption intensity by calculating monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after adoption begins. Developed by Ramp economists for the 2026 AI Jobs Impact Study, this methodology addresses limitations of occupational exposure scores and survey-based adoption measures.

docs.title: Calculation
docs.text:
PEPM_i = (Σ from m=0 to 2 of AI_{i,G_i+m}) / (3 × HC_{i,G_i-1})

Where: - AI_{it} = monthly AI vendor spend - G_i = first month of sustained AI adoption - HC_{i,G_i-1} = baseline headcount in month before adoption

docs.title: Implementation Steps
docs.text:
1. Adoption Definition: First month of earliest three-consecutive-month spell with ≥$100 AI spend monthly
  2. Intensity Measurement: Calculate PEPM using first three post-adoption months
  3. Group Classification: Low intensity = bottom two PEPM terciles, High intensity = top tercile
  4. Comparison Design: Compare earlier adopters to later adopters in same intensity group

docs.title: Advantages Over Alternative Methods
docs.text: Method Limitations PEPM Advantages Occupational exposure scores Vary only across occupations, not firms Measures actual firm adoption decisions Executive surveys Capture awareness not implementation Tracks payment data showing actual usage AI-related job postings Proxy for interest not adoption Measures direct financial commitment Resume AI skills Lagging indicator of adoption Captures immediate spending behavior

  • First three months of spending strongly predicts long-term adoption patterns

docs.title: Epoch score
docs.text: The EPOCH score measures the reliance on human capabilities in various occupations.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The EPOCH score, pwc's proprietary metric, quantifies occupational reliance on human capabilities difficult for AI to replicate. Ranging 0-1, it evaluates dimensions including empathy, creativity, physical dexterity, and face-to-face interaction through job description analysis and expert assessment. Figure 10 of the 2026 report provides definitive validation: new tasks added to AI-exposed roles since 2022 show EPOCH scores 2.5 times higher in the top exposure quartile (0.47) versus bottom quartile (0.19), proving AI shifts work toward human-intensive activities. Figure 11 further demonstrates its significance by showing democratised roles (0.48) and professionalised roles (0.45) maintain substantially higher scores than low exposure roles (0.26), indicating both AI impact pathways increase human reliance. The methodology explains key economic trends: occupations with higher EPOCH scores in AI-exposed roles command greater wage premiums (Figure 15), as human skills become scarcer value drivers. Crucially, the score helps operationalize the ai-job-future-framework's 'AI's limitations' dimension by identifying tasks requiring human oversight. The report shows EPOCH scores are rising fastest in high-exposure roles (Figure 9), with the top quartile's score increasing 116% from 2023-2025. This metric has become essential for organizations mapping future skill requirements, particularly in designing professionalised-jobs and addressing the human elements of 'superstar' company success (Figure 12). Policymakers also use it to target workforce development initiatives where human capabilities provide sustainable competitive advantages.

docs.title: Pwc ai occupational exposure index
docs.text: PwC's proprietary methodology to measure the degree to which different occupations are exposed to AI capabilities.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: PwC's AI Occupational Exposure Index quantifies occupational susceptibility to AI through a multi-dimensional methodology. Ranging 0-1, it analyzes 2,000+ work activities across 800+ occupations, assessing technical feasibility, economic viability, and adoption timelines for AI automation. The 2026 report reveals 74% of jobs have meaningful exposure (quartiles 2-4), with the top quartile experiencing transformative impacts. Figure 3 demonstrates how the index interacts with expertise requirements, showing high-exposure jobs either increase (professionalisation) or decrease (democratization) expertise demands. The methodology underpins critical findings: Figure 7 uses it to segment entry-level job trends, Figure 9 to analyze skill change velocity (top quartile changing 2.2x faster), and Figure 12 to correlate exposure with productivity. Notably, the index evolved to incorporate generative AI capabilities post-2022, explaining accelerated impacts observed after ChatGPT's release. Organizations apply it to identify at-risk roles, prioritize reskilling, and benchmark against industry peers—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' where top-quartile firms achieve 163% productivity growth. The report details sector-specific adaptations (e.g., healthcare's focus on diagnostic support roles), making it versatile for workforce planning. When combined with the epoch-score, the index forms the empirical foundation of the ai-job-future-framework, enabling organizations to systematically address all four framework questions. Its longitudinal design (2012-2025 data) provides unprecedented insight into AI's accelerating labor market transformation.

docs.title: Ai specialist roles
docs.text: Job roles specifically focused on the development, implementation, and maintenance of AI systems, growing eight times faster than total job postings.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI specialist roles are experiencing explosive growth, expanding eight times faster than total job postings according to Figure 16 of the PwC 2026 report. From a 2012 baseline of zero, these roles reached 11.0x growth by 2025 versus 2.0x for total postings, with acceleration intensifying post-2022. Figure 16b shows pervasive sector adoption: Technology, Media and Telecoms leads at 11.4% of sector roles, followed by Health Industries (4.0%), Financial Services (3.0%), and Manufacturing (2.0%). Core responsibilities include AI system architecture, prompt engineering, ethical governance, and domain-specific integration—often blending technical and business skills. Figure 15 confirms these roles command significant wage premiums averaging 62%, with Consumer Markets reaching 118%. The report identifies three growth drivers: urgent demand for AI implementation expertise, the need to address [[ai's limitations]] in quality control and edge cases, and regulatory compliance requirements. Crucially, Figure 12 links this growth to the 'superstar effect', as top-performing AI-exposed companies achieve 163% productivity growth by strategically deploying these specialists. Unlike traditional tech roles, modern AI specialists increasingly operate in hybrid functions (e.g., AI-augmented [[pharmacists]] or [[financial-analysts]]), requiring both domain knowledge and technical proficiency. This trend positions AI specialization as a critical career pathway across the economy, with implications for education systems needing to develop curricula aligned with the ai-job-future-framework.

docs.text: Democratised jobs—where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans—constitute 52% of global postings but show distinct market patterns. docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Entry-level job postings in quartiles with lower AI exposure continue to grow, while those in the highest AI exposure quartile have flatlined since 2022. As documented in multiple studies, these positions represent critical training grounds for developing professional expertise through the habituation process.

docs.title: Contradictory Evidence
docs.text:
Recent research presents seemingly contradictory findings about entry-level job trends:

  • Exposure-based studies: Predict decline in entry-level roles due to AI automation
  • Spending-based research: Shows growth in entry-level roles among high-intensity AI adopters

The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study resolves this contradiction by revealing: - High-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) grew entry-level headcount by 12.0% - Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change - Gains emerged gradually, reaching significance around 6-12 months post-adoption - Growth was broad across functions: engineering, sales, admin, customer service

This explains why the entry-level-squeeze concept remains relevant despite overall growth—entry-level roles are growing only among firms making substantial AI investments.

docs.title: Structural Tensions
docs.text:
Entry-level positions face three competing forces:

  1. Automation pressure: AI systems can perform foundational tasks that traditionally served as training grounds
  2. Capacity development need: Junior staff require opportunities to develop through the habituation process
  3. Strategic value: High-intensity AI adopters recognize entry-level roles as essential for scaling AI-enhanced operations

This creates a bifurcated market where entry-level opportunities are shrinking in low-AI firms but expanding in high-AI firms.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
The industry faces a critical challenge:

  • Traditional pathways: Junior researchers developing through manual analysis are becoming rare
  • New requirements: Entry-level roles increasingly demand human-intensive-skills alongside AI literacy
  • Capacity risk: Over-automation threatens the embodiment-in-skilling and intersubjectivity-in-skilling needed for deep expertise

The ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem study warns that without careful design, AI tools may create capacity-hostile environments where junior researchers miss critical development opportunities.

docs.title: Strategic Framework for Organizations
docs.text: Market research firms should adopt a dual approach:

docs.title: For High-Intensity AI Adopters
docs.text:
• Preserve foundational tasks: Create 'capacity zones' where junior staff develop without AI assistance
  • Structured progression: Gradually increase AI tool complexity as researchers develop
  • Mentorship integration: Pair AI tools with human guidance to maintain intersubjectivity-in-skilling

docs.title: For All Organizations
docs.text:
• Measure capacity development: Track skill progression alongside productivity metrics
  • Design capacity-conducive workflows: Ensure AI tools extend rather than replace the learning journey
  • Value human-intensive-skills: Recognize that AI augmentation increases demand for uniquely human capacities

It explains how the entry-level-squeeze operates within a context of overall growth among high-AI firms, creating a bifurcated job market.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals managing entry-level talent: - Never automate foundational analytical tasks that provide essential habituation - Create clear pathways showing how junior staff progress from manual to AI-enhanced work - Balance AI efficiency with capacity development opportunities - Measure both productivity gains and capacity development outcomes

Without this balanced approach, organizations risk creating researchers who lack the deep intuition needed to navigate complex, novel challenges—precisely where AI systems reach their limits.

docs.title: AI Deskilling and Core Human Capacities
docs.text: Recent research reveals that AI adoption poses specific risks to human-intensive skills through what Ferdman (2026) terms "capacity impoverishment." Unlike skill obsolescence in domains like hunting or basket-weaving, the deskilling of core human capacities diminishes us as humans and undermines our flourishing.

docs.title: Core Capacities at Risk
docs.text:
The following capacities are particularly vulnerable to AI-mediated deskilling:

  • Epistemic capacities: Theoretical rationality (thinking, considering reasons, forming beliefs) and practical rationality (phronesis or wisdom)
  • Social capacities: Moral capacity and abilities for developing meaningful relationships
  • Creative capacity: Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas
  • Volitional capacity: The ability to exert effort, overcome difficulty, and persevere

These capacities differ from technical skills because they are constitutive of human flourishing. As Ferdman explains, "the deskilling of our core human capacities is bad because inadequate development of these capacities can lead to 'capacity impoverishment,' which, in turn, diminishes us as humans."

docs.title: Structural Dimensions of Deskilling
docs.text:
Deskilling is not merely an individual responsibility issue. AI creates systemic conditions that inhibit capacity development through:

  • Capacity-hostile environments: That restrict action possibilities for capacity cultivation
  • Undermined habituation: Short-circuiting the gradual process of skill development
  • Reduced intersubjectivity: Diminishing opportunities for shared valuing of capacities
  • Disembodiment: Limiting physical presence necessary for certain capacities

For market research professionals, this means AI tools that automate data interpretation without preserving opportunities for researchers to develop critical thinking may ultimately undermine the quality of insights produced.

docs.text:
